Chapter Eight: The Ongoing Call to Reform—A Living Tradition.
Let’s talk about something that’s easy to forget but absolutely vital: real reform isn’t just a one-time thing—it’s a journey that never really ends.
Think about it—just like each of us keeps growing and learning, the church is called to keep reflecting, re-examining, and sometimes even reimagining its beliefs, its practices, and how it’s structured. And sure, that can be uncomfortable. Letting go of routines, or facing tough truths, isn’t always simple. But it’s worth it.
A living tradition, at its heart, stays grounded in what matters most—those core principles—while still leaving room for renewal and growth. So, what does that look like in practice?
Well, for starters, it means coming back, again and again, to the basics: the foundational teachings. Are our current actions really lining up with the spirit of the Gospel? Or have we drifted a little?
It also means not being afraid of honest feedback or fresh perspectives. Sometimes, real wisdom comes from tough conversations and listening to voices we don’t always expect.
And maybe most importantly, it means being willing to let go of traditions or habits that no longer help the church’s mission—or its people. That’s not about tossing out everything old, but about asking: what’s truly essential, and what isn’t?
Picture a tree. To keep growing strong, it has to shed its dead branches and send out new shoots. The church, in the same way, needs to prune away what’s lost its life, making space for something new and vibrant to emerge.
Of course, stepping into reform takes real courage. People who ask tough questions or challenge how things have always been done? They might face pushback or get misunderstood. But if you look back through history, you’ll see that real renewal often starts with just a handful of people—folks brave enough to speak the truth, but always with love.
When the church keeps saying “yes” to this ongoing call to reform, it stays alive, relevant, and true to its mission—no matter what generation it finds itself in.
